blurb: What makes something a sport, how stunts really work, the injury numbers, and the legal and Olympic fight over cheer's status.

cards.title: Putting cheer to the sport test

steps.p: Sideline cheer means leading crowd chants at someone else's game. Competitive cheer is different: teams perform a timed routine of stunts, flips, jumps and dance, and judges score it against other teams. The 'is it a sport?' argument is mostly about the competitive kind.

Most definitions share four ingredients: real physical effort, skill that takes years of training, a contest against others, and rules with an official way to pick a winner. Let's check competitive cheer against each one.
steps.analogy: Like a recipe: if all four ingredients are in the bowl, you're baking the same cake, whatever the box says.

steps.p: A competitive routine lasts about two and a half minutes of nonstop tumbling, lifting and throwing teammates, jumping and dancing — while smiling and staying in time. Athletes train strength, flexibility and stamina much like gymnasts do.
steps.analogy: Like running a fast 800 metres while juggling, and having to look relaxed the whole way.

steps.p: Back flips, twisting flips and throwing a teammate high into the air take years of practice. A mistake can mean a hard fall, so technique is drilled over and over before it's ever tried in front of judges.
steps.analogy: Like learning to drive: nobody gets the keys to a race car on day one.

steps.p: Competitive cheer has rulebooks listing which skills are allowed at each level, trained judges, score sheets and a ladder of championships — right up to a world championships run by an international governing body.

cards.aside: By the usual tests, competitive cheer passes. The real arguments are about history, image and official labels — later lessons cover those.

cards.q: Which kind of cheerleading is mostly at the centre of the 'is it a sport?' debate?
options: Competitive cheer, where teams perform judged routines against each other
Leading chants from the stands as an ordinary fan
Dance-only routines performed at halftime shows
Mascots performing in costume at games
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 1.
cards.why: Competitive cheer. It is its own event with judges, scores and winners — the contest ingredient that sideline cheer lacks. That's why most of the case for 'sport' rests on it.

cards.statement: Under the common four-part test, an activity needs a ball or a goal to count as a sport.
cards.hint: Check the four ingredients in step 2.
cards.why: False. The test asks for effort, skill, a contest and rules — nothing about balls or goals. Gymnastics, diving and figure skating are judged sports with neither.

cards.q: Which ingredient of the 'sport' test does sideline cheer most clearly lack?
options: A contest — sideline squads aren't scored against rivals
Physical effort — it needs no fitness at all
Skill — anyone can do it without training
Teamwork — members perform alone
cards.hint: What does cheering for someone else's team not include?
cards.why: A contest. Sideline squads can be fit and highly skilled, but they support another team rather than competing for their own result. That's the main reason they're treated differently.

cards.title: The first cheerleaders were men.
cards.detail: In 1898 a University of Minnesota student, Johnny Campbell, led the crowd in an organised chant and is often called the first cheerleader. Women joined in large numbers from the 1920s onward, especially when many men left for World War II.

cards.q: Roughly how long is a typical competitive cheer routine?
options: About two and a half minutes
About 20 seconds
About 15 minutes
As long as a whole football game
cards.why: About two and a half minutes. It's short, but packed: stunts, pyramids, tumbling, jumps and dance follow each other without a break, which is why stamina matters so much.

cards.statement: Competitive cheer has a world championships run by an international governing body.
cards.hint: Look at the last item in the flow in step 5.
cards.why: True. National teams compete at world championships organised by the International Cheer Union. Having a governing body, shared rules and championships is one of the classic marks of a sport.

cards.title: The physics and teamwork of a stunt

steps.p: A stunt group usually has a flyer (the person lifted into the air), two bases (who hold and throw the flyer) and a backspot (who stands behind, helps lift and guards the flyer's head and neck).
Bases drive the flyer upward with their legs, like a squat jump, then lock their arms overhead. Lifting on exactly the same count matters as much as raw strength, so groups count every move out loud.
steps.analogy: Like two people carrying a sofa upstairs: if one pushes early, the whole thing tips.

steps.p: A flyer keeps their body tight and rigid, balances on one foot in teammates' hands and holds poses with their feet above the bases' heads. A rigid body is much easier to hold steady and to catch than a floppy one.
steps.analogy: It's easy to balance a broom upright on your palm — try that with a rope.

steps.p: Bases lock hands to make a platform, the flyer steps in, and the group throws them high into the air. The flyer does a trick at the top, then is caught lying flat in the bases' arms, called a cradle.
When catching, bases bend their knees and arms to slow the flyer down over a longer moment. Spreading the stop over more time means a smaller force on everyone's body.
steps.analogy: Like catching a raw egg: you move your hands back with it instead of stopping it dead.

steps.p: Teams also tumble — handsprings, back flips and twisting flips on a springy floor, just like gymnasts. Jumps such as the toe touch, with legs split out to the sides, need flexible hips and explosive leg power.

cards.aside: A stunt is a team lift: if any one person is late, the whole group wobbles.

cards.q: In a stunt group, who stands behind to protect the flyer's head and neck?
options: The backspot
The flyer
The front base
The head judge
cards.hint: Check the four roles in step 1.
cards.why: The backspot. They stand behind the stunt, help lift and watch the flyer's upper body, because a fall onto the head or neck is the most dangerous kind.

cards.statement: In a stunt, the bases' timing matters as much as their raw strength.
cards.hint: Think of the sofa analogy in step 2.
cards.why: True. Two bases lifting on different counts tip the flyer off balance, however strong they are. That's why groups count out loud and rehearse the same lift hundreds of times.

cards.q: Why do bases bend their knees and arms as they catch a falling flyer?
options: It spreads the stop over more time, so the force is smaller
It makes the flyer fall a little faster
Judges award extra points for deep knee bends
It lets the bases see the flyer more clearly
cards.hint: Look at the stiff-versus-soft comparison in step 5.
cards.why: To spread the stop over more time. Bringing a moving body to rest takes the same total 'push' either way; doing it over a longer moment makes the peak force smaller and gentler on joints.

cards.title: In a full stunt, a flyer's head can be higher than a basketball hoop.
cards.detail: In an extension the bases hold the flyer's feet at arm's length overhead, around two metres up. Add the flyer's own height and their head is often above three metres — taller than a standard hoop.

cards.q: Why are flyers taught to keep their whole body tight and rigid in the air?
options: A rigid body is easier to balance and catch
Tight muscles make the flyer weigh less
Rules require flyers to stand perfectly still
It stops the flyer from feeling dizzy
cards.hint: Remember the broom and the rope.
cards.why: It's easier to balance and catch. A stiff body moves as one piece, so bases can steady it from a few points. A loose body bends and shifts, making it far harder to control.

cards.statement: At the end of a basket toss, the flyer is usually caught in a cradle rather than landing on the floor.
cards.hint: Check the last item in the flow in step 4.
cards.why: True. The bases catch the flyer lying flat in their arms. Landing on the floor from that height would be far too risky, which is why the catch is part of the skill.

cards.title: How cheer is judged — and what it costs bodies

steps.p: Judges score each part — stunts, pyramids, tosses, tumbling, jumps and dance — on how hard it is and how cleanly it's done. Points come off for falls and other mistakes. The highest total wins.

Teams compete in numbered levels. Lower levels ban the riskiest skills; higher levels allow more. Rulebooks say exactly which flips and stunts are legal at each level, so teams compete against others with similar skills.
steps.analogy: Like belts in karate: you don't spar a black belt on your first day.

steps.p: Most cheer injuries are sprains and strains — ankles, wrists, backs — like in many sports. But because people are lifted and thrown, a fall from height can cause concussions or head and neck injuries. Stunts cause a large share of injuries.

right.title: Rarer but serious
points: Head and neck injuries from falls

steps.p: Studies of US high-school sports have found cheer's overall injury rate is lower than many sports, such as football or girls' soccer. Yet cheer has made up a large share of the most serious injuries among female athletes. Both can be true at once.
steps.analogy: Like flying versus driving: fewer accidents per trip, but the rare one can be severe.

steps.p: When a school or state calls cheer a sport, that usually brings what sports get: qualified coaches, safety rules, practice limits, athletic trainers and injury tracking. In 2012 the AAP, a major US doctors' group, urged exactly this.

cards.aside: The 'is it a sport?' question isn't just about pride — it decides who looks after the athletes.

cards.q: In a competitive routine, what usually happens when a flyer falls?
options: The team loses points as a deduction
Nothing — only the dance section is judged
The team is automatically disqualified
The routine restarts from the beginning
cards.hint: Look at the scoring flow in step 1.
cards.why: A deduction. Judges take points off for falls and other errors, so a team that attempts harder skills must also hit them cleanly. Risk and reward are balanced in the score.

cards.q: Why are cheer competitions split into numbered levels?
options: So teams compete against others with similar, permitted skills
So routines at higher levels can be shorter
Because judges can only score one level per day
To keep sideline and competitive squads apart
cards.hint: Think of the karate belts in step 2.
cards.why: To match teams by skill. Each level has its own list of legal skills, so beginners aren't pushed into dangerous tricks and teams are ranked against fair rivals.

cards.statement: Most cheerleading injuries are serious head and neck injuries.
cards.hint: Look at the 'Common' side in step 3.
cards.why: False. Most are sprains and strains, as in other sports. Head and neck injuries are rarer — but because they can be so serious, they drive much of the safety debate.

cards.title: A major US doctors' group asked for cheer to be called a sport — for safety.
cards.detail: In 2012 the American Academy of Pediatrics said school sports bodies should label cheerleading a sport, so cheerleaders get the qualified coaching, rules, medical care and injury tracking other athletes get.

cards.statement: Research suggests cheer has a fairly low overall injury rate but a large share of the most serious injuries among female athletes.
cards.hint: Step 4 explains how both can be true.
cards.why: True. Per practice or game, cheerleaders get hurt less often than athletes in many sports. But falls from stunts mean that when injuries happen, a larger share are severe.

cards.q: Which part of cheer causes many of its injuries?
options: Stunts and pyramids, where people are lifted and thrown
The dance section near the end
Chanting, which strains the voice
Stretching during the warm-up
cards.why: Stunts and pyramids. Lifting and throwing people means bodies fall from height — the source of a large share of injuries, and most of the serious ones.

steps.p: Critics point to cheer's roots in supporting other teams, the focus on smiles and appearance, and sideline squads that never compete. To them, cheer exists to serve another sport rather than to win its own contest.
steps.analogy: Like asking whether the orchestra at a ballet is part of the ballet or a separate show.

steps.p: Title IX is a 1972 US law requiring schools to give women and girls equal chances to play sports. Some colleges wanted to count cheer squads toward that. In 2010 a US judge ruled one college's competitive cheer didn't count yet: it wasn't organised enough, with no settled season, rules or governing body.

items: 2010: judge says cheer doesn't count yet

steps.p: In response, cheer-based college formats were built to look like other sports, with fixed seasons and head-to-head scoring. In 2020 the NCAA, which runs US college sport, named one of them — acrobatics and tumbling — an 'emerging sport' for women.
steps.analogy: Like rewriting a hobby club's rules so it qualifies for a proper league.

steps.p: In 2016 the IOC gave the International Cheer Union provisional recognition, then full recognition in 2021. That makes cheer an official sport in the Olympic movement — but recognition doesn't put it on the Games programme.

items: Not yet: a place at the Games

steps.p: By the usual tests and the Olympic movement's own decision, competitive cheer is a sport. Sideline cheer is better seen as a support role, though still athletic. Official labels still differ by school, US state and country.

cards.q: What did the IOC's 2021 decision mean for cheerleading?
options: It became a fully recognised sport, though not yet on the Games programme
It was added as a medal event at the next Olympics
It was banned from international competition
It was merged into gymnastics as one event
cards.hint: Read the last item of the timeline in step 4.
cards.why: Full recognition, not a Games slot. Recognition means the IOC accepts cheer's governing body as part of the Olympic movement. Getting into the Games is a separate decision.

cards.statement: Being recognised by the IOC means a sport automatically appears at the next Olympic Games.
cards.hint: Step 4 separates recognition from the Games programme.
cards.why: False. Many recognised sports have never been on the programme. Each Games' line-up is chosen separately, so recognition is a step toward the Olympics, not a ticket in.

cards.q: Why did a 2010 US court say one college's competitive cheer team didn't yet count under Title IX?
options: It wasn't organised like a sport yet: no settled season, rules or governing body
The judge found cheerleading too dangerous for women
The team included too many male members
Title IX only covers sports that use a ball
cards.why: It wasn't organised enough yet. The ruling wasn't that cheer is too easy — it was that the team lacked the structure of a real varsity sport, such as a proper season and shared rules.

cards.title: Cheer has its own world championships, with national teams from dozens of countries.
cards.detail: The International Cheer Union, founded in 2004, runs world championships where national teams compete in judged routines, just like other international sports.

cards.q: Which comparison best fits sideline cheer?
options: A marching band: skilled, but supporting another event
A referee: enforcing the rules of the game
A coach: choosing the team's tactics
A spectator: simply watching the game
cards.hint: Look at the right side of the comparison in step 5.
cards.why: A marching band. Both take real training and athletic effort, but both exist to support someone else's game rather than to win a contest of their own.

cards.title: Watch a routine like a judge
cards.body: Find a video of a competitive cheer routine. Watch it once for fun, then again counting stunts, flips and falls. You'll see how much is packed into two and a half minutes.
cards.challenge: In one routine, count every time a flyer is lifted or thrown — and watch how the bases soften each catch.
